planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in early fall or just after spring bloom; divide congested clumps every two to three years to keep the leafy-calyx trait and named colors consistent.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Jack-in-the-Green Group primroses are a centuries-old class of English primrose distinguished by an enlarged, leaf-like green calyx that flares out beneath each flower like a ruff or collar, echoing the leaf-costumed May Day folk figure the group is named for. Flower color varies among individual selections within the group, spanning yellow, red, and purple shades, but the oversized leafy collar surrounding every bloom is the constant, instantly recognizable trait. Because the collar character can be lost in seedlings, plants are kept true by division rather than by seed. Divide crowded clumps every two to three years right after flowering to maintain vigor and increase stock.

common_name: Marie Crousse Primrose (Lilac Picotee Double Primrose)

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in early fall; this historic double sets little viable seed and is propagated only by division to keep the picotee edge true.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; 'Marie Crousse' is one of the oldest surviving double primroses still in cultivation, a French-raised selection dating to around the turn of the twentieth century, bearing fully packed lilac-mauve flowers edged in a fine white picotee margin above crinkled rosettes of green leaves. Bloom runs from late winter into mid-spring, and the picotee edging is most distinct in cool weather. Like other historic doubles, it must be increased by division rather than seed to keep the distinctive edged coloring consistent. Divide congested clumps every two to three years right after flowering to renew vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in early fall; propagate only by division to keep the striped petal pattern consistent, since it is a clonal double.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; 'Miss Massey' is a Victorian-era double primrose carrying fully packed, ruffled flowers streaked and flecked with lilac-purple over a paler lavender-cream ground, a broken or feathered pattern rather than a solid color. It flowers from late winter into mid-spring over neat rosettes of crinkled green foliage and is chiefly grown by collectors of heirloom florists' primroses. Because the striped pattern does not come true from seed, plants are maintained only by division. Divide congested clumps every two to three years after flowering to renew vigor and increase stock.

common_name: Quaker's Bonnet Primrose (Lilacina Plena Double Primrose)

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in early fall; this ancient double sets no viable seed and is propagated only by division.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; sold under the old folk name Quaker's Bonnet as well as its Latin tag 'Lilacina Plena', this is one of the longest-documented double primroses in English gardens, producing fully packed, soft lavender-blue flowers with no visible yellow eye above crinkled rosettes of green leaves. It blooms from late winter into mid-spring and has been passed down among collectors of historic florists' flowers for generations. Because it does not set seed, the clone is kept going only by regular division. Divide congested clumps every two to three years right after flowering to maintain vigor.

common_name: Our Pat Primrose (Dark Red Double Primrose)

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in early fall; increase only by division to keep the deep red double flowers true.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; 'Our Pat' is a named double primrose grown by heirloom-primrose collectors for its densely packed, dark red to maroon rosette-form flowers held just above crinkled green foliage from late winter into mid-spring. The deep, velvety color reads darker than most double primroses, giving it a moodier presence at the edge of a shaded border. As a clonal double it does not come true from seed and must be increased by division. Divide congested clumps every two to three years after flowering to maintain vigor.

common_name: Bon Accord Purple Primrose (Scottish Heirloom Double Primrose)

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in early fall; propagate only by division to keep this early-twentieth-century Scottish double true.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; 'Bon Accord Purple' belongs to the Bon Accord strain of double primroses first raised in Aberdeen, Scotland in the early twentieth century and named for the city's motto. It produces fully packed, rounded, rich purple flowers over neat rosettes of crinkled green leaves from late winter into mid-spring, one of several named color forms within the historic Bon Accord group. Because the Bon Accord doubles set little fertile seed, they are kept in circulation by division among heirloom-primrose collectors. Divide congested clumps every two to three years right after flowering to renew vigor.
